# The Girl Who Wanted More

## Part One: Hunger of a Different Kind

Mara had always been different.

Growing up in a cramped apartment on the edge of a struggling town, she had known hunger in the ordinary sense — the kind that gnaws at your stomach when the cupboards are bare and payday is still three days away. Her mother worked two jobs. Her father had left before she could remember his face. There were four children and never quite enough of anything.

But Mara carried a different kind of hunger alongside the practical one.

While her siblings dreamed of escaping their thin circumstances — of big cities, good jobs, comfortable lives — Mara dreamed of *weight*. Of substance. Of taking up space in the world in a way she never had. She was nineteen and weighed barely ninety pounds, her frame slight and angular, her clothes always hanging loose no matter how tightly she cinched her belt.

She had always envied people who were large. Not in a cruel way. In a genuinely aching, wistful way. They seemed *anchored* to her. Rooted. Like the wind could not simply carry them away. Like the world had to acknowledge them, had to *move around them* rather than passing through them as if they were barely there.

Her family noticed her habits. She ate more than anyone her size should have been able to manage, yet her body seemed reluctant to hold onto anything. Doctors had no satisfying answers. *Fast metabolism*, they said, shrugging. *You'll fill out eventually.* She never did.

By nineteen, she had stopped waiting for eventually.

She was going to make it happen herself.

---

## Part Two: The Arrangement

Kowalski's Family Restaurant sat on a corner of Drebben Street that had seen better decades. The sign was missing two letters. The awning had faded from red to a tired pink. The windows were clean enough, but the overall impression was of a place that had simply *endured* rather than thrived.

Mara had walked past it a hundred times. She knew its reputation. Everyone in the neighborhood did.

The food was not good.

This was not a matter of opinion or snobbery. It was simply a fact that the neighborhood had quietly agreed upon. Mr. Kowalski, the owner, was a heavyset man in his sixties who had inherited the restaurant from his own father and had never quite developed the passion for cooking that the inheritance demanded. His portions were large but his recipes were tired. His sauces were thick in the wrong ways. His bread arrived at the table already staling. People came occasionally, out of habit or proximity or the particular laziness of a Tuesday evening, but they rarely came back with enthusiasm, and they rarely finished their plates.

The kitchen threw away extraordinary amounts of food.

Mara had thought about this for a long time before she walked through the door.

She found Mr. Kowalski behind the bar on a slow Wednesday afternoon, doing his accounts with the expression of a man losing an argument with mathematics.

*I want to work for you*, she said.

He looked up and took in her slight frame with the automatic skepticism of someone who had hired waitresses before. *You got experience?*

*Some*, she said, which was a flexible truth. She had helped at a church supper twice.

He named a wage. She shook her head.

*I don't want money*, she said.

He put his pen down.

She laid out her proposal clearly and without embarrassment. She had nowhere to live — which was mostly true, her current situation being a friend's sofa that was wearing out its welcome. She needed a roof and she needed food. She would work hard, keep the place clean, take any shift he needed covered. In exchange, she wanted the back storeroom to sleep in, and she wanted the kitchen leftovers. All of them. Whatever didn't go out to customers, whatever came back from tables, whatever was destined for the bin.

Mr. Kowalski was quiet for a moment.

He was not an unkind man, but he was primarily a practical one. What she was describing would cost him almost nothing. Labor, these days, was not cheap. And the food — the food was genuinely going to waste regardless. He thought about the accounting he had just been doing, and the numbers that kept refusing to improve.

*You'd sleep in the storeroom?*

*I've slept in worse*, she said, which was true.

*And you're sure about the wage?*

*Room and food*, she said. *That's all I want.*

He extended his hand. She shook it.

She moved in that same evening, arranging a cot between the shelving units, hanging her few belongings on a hook behind the door. The storeroom smelled of old cardboard and dried herbs. She found it perfectly comfortable.

That night, after the last customers left and the kitchen was being wiped down, she sat at the prep counter and ate.

---

## Part Three: The Work of Becoming

The arrangement suited everyone in the beginning.

Mara was a capable waitress once she settled in. She learned the menu quickly, moved efficiently between tables, and had a natural warmth with customers that Mr. Kowalski, who was gruff by default, genuinely could not manufacture. Tips improved slightly. The regulars who came on Thursday evenings started asking for her specifically.

And the food — there was so much food.

Because the restaurant's quality remained consistently mediocre, the leftover situation remained consistently generous. Mara ate what came back from the tables. She ate what the kitchen prepared in excess. She worked out an understanding with the evening cook, a quiet man named Tibor, who learned not to be startled by her appetite and eventually began setting aside portions he knew she would want.

She ate with focus and with joy.

Breakfast was whatever bread and pastry hadn't moved. Lunch, if she wasn't on shift, was assembled from the previous night's remainders. After the dinner service, she sat in the kitchen and worked through the accumulated surplus with calm and methodical pleasure.

Weeks passed. Then months.

The changes were gradual at first, and then less so.

Her face filled out. The sharp angles of her cheeks and jawline softened into curves. Her clothes, which had always hung, began to fit, and then to strain, and then she had to replace them. Her arms lost their bony definition. Her stomach rounded. Her movements changed — slower, heavier, more deliberate — in a way that she did not find inconvenient so much as *satisfying*.

She was becoming substantial.

She was taking up space.

Mr. Kowalski noticed, of course. He said nothing. It was not his business. She was doing her work, his labor costs were minimal, and if she was eating well on the job, that was hardly unusual in the restaurant industry.

The months continued.

---

## Part Four: The World Grows Smaller

By the end of the first year, Mara had gained weight that transformed her appearance entirely.

By the end of the second, she had become someone her mother would not immediately have recognized.

By the middle of the third year, problems began.

Not dramatic problems. Quiet ones, at first. The chairs in the restaurant were no longer comfortable for her. She began to avoid sitting when possible, then found standing for a full shift increasingly difficult, and finally arrived at a compromise where she managed the counter and the nearby tables while the other staff — there were two part-time servers by now — handled the rest of the floor.

Her movement through the restaurant had always been fluid. It became careful. She learned to angle herself through the space between tables, to move sideways through the kitchen, to be thoughtful about which paths she took.

Then she stopped waiting tables entirely, transitioning by unspoken mutual agreement into a role that was harder to define — part hostess, part cashier, part presence.

She was content.

She was more than content. She felt, for the first time in her life, as though she occupied the world in the way she had always wanted. She was not invisible. She was not insubstantial. She was *there*, undeniably, in a way that could not be overlooked or passed through.

The restaurant hummed along around her. The food remained mediocre. The leftovers remained plentiful.

She ate.

---

## Part Five: Thresholds

The door problem announced itself on an ordinary Tuesday morning.

Mara had slept in her storeroom — which had been gradually reorganized over the years to accommodate her, shelves pushed back, the cot replaced with a wider mattress on the floor — and was making her way to the bathroom before the breakfast prep began.

She turned sideways in the hallway, as she had learned to do.

The angle was not quite right.

She adjusted.

She stood in the hallway for a long moment, attempting different approaches with the patience of someone solving a practical problem, and arrived at the conclusion that the doorframe was no longer negotiable.

She was not frightened, precisely. She stood in the hallway and took stock of her situation with the same practical clarity she had applied to her arrangement with Mr. Kowalski three years earlier. She catalogued her options. She found them significantly reduced.

The bathroom was inaccessible.

The front door of the restaurant, wider than the interior doors, she had already stopped attempting several months ago.

The kitchen door she could still manage, barely, with care.

She was, for practical purposes, confined to the main dining room, the kitchen, and the storeroom. Three connected spaces. The restaurant was her world now in a way that was no longer metaphorical.

She stood in the hallway and was honest with herself about what this meant.

Then she went back to the kitchen and ate breakfast.

---

## Part Six: Difficult Realities

What followed was a period that Mara would later — in the private accounting she did with herself during the long quiet hours — classify as *difficult*.

The bathroom situation had no comfortable resolution. She managed as best she could with buckets and cleaning, but the restaurant was a restaurant, a place people came to eat, and the smell of even carefully managed human necessity eventually reached the dining room regardless of her efforts.

Customers began to notice.

A few said nothing, simply paid and left and did not return. A few others were less diplomatic. A family who came every Sunday for a late lunch stopped coming after a particular Sunday when the father made a complaint to Mr. Kowalski that Mara, at the counter, could hear clearly.

Mr. Kowalski became increasingly strained.

He was not cruel to her. He had never been a cruel man. But he had also not imagined, three years ago, that their arrangement would arrive here. He had not thought carefully about trajectories. Neither, if she was honest, had she — or rather, she had thought only about the destination she wanted, not about all the practical geography between here and there.

He hired a cleaning service to come twice a week. This helped, at a cost that his margins could not comfortably absorb.

The regulars thinned. New customers, drawn in by a local review he had paid too much for, came once and did not return. Word traveled, as word does in neighborhoods where everyone knows everyone's history.

The accounts, always marginal, became critical.

Mara watched this happen with a grief she had not anticipated. She liked Mr. Kowalski. She was grateful to him. She had not intended to be the weight that sank him, which struck her, alone at night, as a thought with edges sharp enough to cut.

But she could not undo what she had become. And she could not leave.

---

## Part Seven: The Last Day of Business

It was a Thursday when Mr. Kowalski sat down across from her at the corner table — the one with the extra space that she had claimed as her own — and told her.

He had the look of a man who had made a decision and was not going to unmake it, which she recognized because she had worn that look herself, three years ago, walking through his door.

The bank, he said. The suppliers. The numbers.

He was sorry.

She told him she understood. She told him, and meant it, that he had been fair with her and she was grateful.

He asked her — carefully, gently, aware of the difficulty — what she would do.

She looked at him steadily and said nothing, because they both understood the answer. There was nothing to say about what she would do, because there was nothing she could do, not in any practical sense. She could not do anything *outside* this building any longer. The question had no real answer.

He looked away first.

He came back two more times over the following weeks, bringing food, and she understood these visits for what they were — obligation and decency intermingled — and was grateful for them. Then the visits stopped, and she understood that too.

---

## Part Eight: Alone

The restaurant was quiet in its abandonment in a way that was entirely different from quiet at closing time.

Closing time quiet was temporary. It had the quality of held breath. This was something else — a permanent settling, a silence that had stopped waiting for noise to return.

Mara sat in her corner and considered her circumstances with the same honesty she had applied to every other stage of this journey.

She had wanted to be substantial. She had wanted to take up space, to be rooted, to be impossible to overlook or pass through. She had understood these desires and had pursued them deliberately and had largely achieved them.

The cost of them — she had not totaled the cost in advance, the way you sometimes fail to add up a bill until it arrives.

She thought about her mother working two jobs in the cramped apartment. She thought about her siblings who had wanted to escape their thin circumstances and had, as far as she knew, managed it. She thought about the word *escape* and the word *anchor* and how she had always thought these were opposites, and how she now understood they were sometimes the same thing — that the thing that roots you is also the thing that holds you.

The kitchen still had inventory, abandoned by a bankruptcy that had moved faster than anyone cleared shelves. She had water from the tap, which still ran. She was not going to starve.

She sat in the dim restaurant in the long afternoons when the light came golden and sideways through the windows that no one was cleaning anymore, and she was honest with herself, and she was — this surprised her — not entirely unhappy.

She was undeniably *here*. Undeniably present. Undeniably occupying her portion of the world in a way that could not be disputed.

She had wanted to matter, to take up space, to be real in the way that large, rooted things are real.

She had gotten her wish.

She sat in the abandoned restaurant in the golden afternoon light and understood, with the particular clarity that comes after all the alternatives have been accounted for, that wishes granted without wisdom have their own kind of weight —

and that weight, too, she had asked for.

---

*The end.*
